name: WORKIVA CLASS A

priced.reason: not a repriceable fcff name or no growth supplied

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: The strongest case for a number rather than a refusal is that the BOX arithmetic I used charges Workiva the full replacement cost of dilution forever, at today's share price, which is the most punitive possible reading. If revenue compounds mid-teens and stock compensation is held flat in dollars - which is what a company hitting its margin target a year early is telling you it is doing - the dilution offset falls as a share of a growing cash flow every single year. Under that path owner earnings grow far faster than the 19% top line, and the +27% requirement is met not by heroics but by arithmetic. On that reading the refusal is the error and Workiva is cheap.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: Stock compensation in absolute dollars over the next four quarters against revenue. If SBC stays near $123M while revenue goes from $885M to $1.04B and then higher, the bull's mechanism is working and the gap between guided FCF and owner earnings closes on its own. If SBC grows with revenue, it does not.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Partly, and it supports the bull. `sbc_series` runs [$98.8M, $102.2M, $122.9M] oldest to newest - so SBC grew 20% in the newest year, faster than revenue's 19.7%, which argues AGAINST the bull. But the 1,300bp of non-GAAP margin expansion and the 2027 target being hit a year early are real and are in the guidance, and the share count is genuinely shrinking, which is the single best evidence that management is treating the comp as a cost. The two readings point in opposite directions and I could not resolve them.
devils_advocate.unresolved: How much of the ~21% free cash flow margin is a working-capital or deferred-revenue build rather than earnings - Workiva's subscription billings are front-loaded and I could not decompose the guided figure. I also note that `shares_asof` and `shares_source` are both NULL in the extract, so the 56,272,517 shares the model uses has no provenance; it happens to reconcile to the Class A plus Class B weighted averages, but that is luck rather than a verified count.

what_changed: Q2 2026 (filed 2026-08-04) beat the high end of revenue guidance, delivered 1,300bp of year-over-year non-GAAP operating margin expansion, and set full-year 2026 free cash flow margin guidance at ~21% of $1.04B of revenue. The company reached GAAP profitability ($12.6M of net income in Q2 against a $0.35 loss per share a year earlier). Nothing structural: no acquisition, no financing, no item 1.01/2.01/3.02 8-K. The 2026 convertible notes mature in August 2026 and were carried at $71.2M current at the balance sheet date.
consensus_case: Workiva is a 19%-growth compliance platform whose margins have inflected hard, and the price reflects the inflection rather than the trailing cash flow. Q2 2026 delivered 19% growth in both subscription and total revenue while non-GAAP operating margin beat the high end of guidance by 180bp - a 1,300 basis point improvement over Q2 of last year - and management said this positions them to hit the 2027 medium-term 18% operating-margin target a full year early. Full-year 2026 guidance is revenue of $1.040-1.044B, GAAP operating margin of 5.7-5.8%, non-GAAP operating margin of approximately 18%, GAAP diluted EPS of $1.21-1.22, and a FREE CASH FLOW MARGIN OF APPROXIMATELY 21% - roughly $219M, against a three-year historical mean of $98.4M. A company doubling free cash flow while growing revenue 19% and turning GAAP-profitable is not obviously mispriced at $4.05B of enterprise value.
base_case_rationale: I cannot narrow this to a number, and the reason is that the two defensible bases are 2.2x apart and both are defensible. The engine's $106.7M base is the three-year mean of cfo-capex [$68.8M, $86.3M, $138.0M] plus a $9.0M interest add-back, and the `possible_peak_cycle_base` flag calls the newest year a peak - which is the ITRI error, because the series is monotonic and the company guides the newest level to rise a further 59% to ~$219M this year. Correcting for that alone takes the required growth from +26.8% to +7.3%, which would make Workiva look cheap. But Workiva's free cash flow is not owner earnings: stock compensation is $122.9M, 110% of the engine's base and 56% of guided free cash flow, and reported FCF adds every dollar of it back. Per the BOX rule I went and got the net share count. Basic weighted-average shares were 55,638,926 in Q2 2026 against 56,076,723 in Q2 2025, and 55,259,608 in H1 2026 against 56,133,286 in H1 2025 - the count is FALLING 1.6% year over year net of all compensation, so unlike Q2 Holdings the comp IS being paid for. But paying for it consumes essentially the whole of it: offsetting ~1.7M shares a year of comp issuance at $72.84 costs roughly $122M, so owner earnings are about $219M - $122M = $97M, plus the $9M add-back, or $106M - which lands almost exactly back on the engine's base by coincidence, and requires +27.2% growth. The answer is therefore +7.3% required if you underwrite guided FCF and +27.2% if you underwrite owner earnings; at a defensible SaaS beta the expensed end reaches +30.1%. A 20-point span on one treatment is not a valuation.
key_risks: the answer spans +7.3% required growth (guided free cash flow) to +30.1% (owner earnings at a defensible discount rate) on one accounting choice
stock compensation of $122.9M is 110% of the engine's FCFF base and grew 20% in the newest year, faster than revenue
beta is 0.62 with an R-squared of 0.067, so the 9.18% WACC is barely a measurement; at a defensible SaaS beta the requirement rises 3 points
shareholders' equity is NEGATIVE $97.1M and $768.6M of convertible notes sit ahead of the equity, $71.2M of it maturing August 2026
watch_for: stock compensation in absolute dollars against revenue over the next four quarters - the one number that collapses the range
whether the FY2026 21% free cash flow margin is delivered, and how much of it is deferred-revenue build
the August 2026 convertible maturity being settled in cash rather than shares
